'''Christina Maria Agapakis''' is a [[Synthetic biology|synthetic biologist]] and science writer. She is the former Creative Director of the biotechnology company [[Ginkgo Bioworks]].

== Education and early life ==
Agapakis received her [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 2006 from [[Yale University]] in molecular, cellular, and developmental biology. She then attended [[Harvard University]], where she received her PhD in biological and biomedical sciences under the mentorship of [[Pamela Silver]].<ref name=phd/> Her thesis, on ''Biological Design Principles for Synthetic Biology'', centered on identifying and utilizing design principles for bioengineering, keeping in mind the evolutionary and ecological contexts under which genes and genetic pathways were being modified or newly synthesized.<ref name=phd>{{cite thesis|first=Christina|last=Agapakis|title=Biological Design Principles for Synthetic Biology|degree=PhD|oclc=1011273718|year=2011|id={{ProQuest|881069635}}|url=https://hollis.harvard.edu/permalink/f/1mdq5o5/TN_cdi_proquest_journals_881069635|website=harvard.edu|publisher=Harvard University}}</ref> 

==Career and research==
Agapakis worked to engineer [[Photosynthesis|photosynthetic]] bacteria to invade animal cells, essentially giving animals cells [[chloroplast]]s, and also engineered bacteria to produce [[hydrogen fuel]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Silver|first1=Pamela A.|last2=Way|first2=Jeffrey C.|last3=Megason|first3=Sean G.|last4=Lieberman|first4=Tami D.|last5=Noche|first5=Ramil R.|last6=Niederholtmeyer|first6=Henrike|last7=Agapakis|first7=Christina M.|date=2011-04-20|title=Towards a Synthetic Chloroplast|journal=PLOS ONE|language=en|volume=6|issue=4|article-number=e18877|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0018877|issn=1932-6203|pmc=3080389|pmid=21533097|bibcode=2011PLoSO...618877A|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Agapakis|first1=Christina M.|last2=Ducat|first2=Daniel C.|last3=Boyle|first3=Patrick M.|last4=Wintermute|first4=Edwin H.|last5=Way|first5=Jeffrey C.|last6=Silver|first6=Pamela A.|date=2010-02-25|title=Insulation of a synthetic hydrogen metabolism circuit in bacteria|journal=Journal of Biological Engineering|volume=4|issue=1|page=3|doi=10.1186/1754-1611-4-3|issn=1754-1611|pmc=2847965|pmid=20184755 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Her thesis covers a range of work she pursued during her doctoral career, including mentoring a Harvard [[IGEM competition]] team in 2010, which developed an open source toolkit for plant engineering known as the Harvard {{proper name|iGarden}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://2010.igem.org/Team:Harvard|title=Team:Harvard - 2010.igem.org|website=2010.igem.org|access-date=2018-12-21}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Boyle|first1=Patrick M.|last2=Burrill|first2=Devin R.|last3=Inniss|first3=Mara C.|last4=Agapakis|first4=Christina M.|last5=Deardon|first5=Aaron|last6=DeWerd|first6=Jonathan G.|last7=Gedeon|first7=Michael A.|last8=Quinn|first8=Jacqueline Y.|last9=Paull|first9=Morgan L.|date=2012-12-01|title=A BioBrick compatible strategy for genetic modification of plants|journal=Journal of Biological Engineering|volume=6|issue=1|page=8|doi=10.1186/1754-1611-6-8|issn=1754-1611|pmc=3537565|pmid=22716313 |doi-access=free }}</ref> She also discussed a project called "Selfmade" at the intersection of science and art, which focused on the microbial ecology of cheese and the human body. She worked with artist and odor expert [[Sissel Tolaas]] during her Synthetic Aesthetics residency, collecting bacteria samples from the belly buttons, feet, mouths, and tears of creatives to engineer 11 "human cheeses."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2013/12/131202-human-cheese-food-biology-weird-gastronomy/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131204003253/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2013/12/131202-human-cheese-food-biology-weird-gastronomy/|archive-date=December 4, 2013|title="Human Cheese" Only the First Course for Odd Cheeses|date=2013-12-04|website=National Geographic News|access-date=2018-12-21}}</ref> The project was exhibited at the "Grow Your Own" exhibition at the Dublin [[Science Gallery]] and was meant more as a thought experiment than a culinary one.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2013/oct/28/grow-your-own-synthetic-biology|title=Grow Your Own: where scientists and artists are shaking up creation|last=Wainwright|first=Oliver|date=2013-10-28|work=The Guardian|access-date=2018-12-21|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

Following her PhD, Agapakis began a [[postdoctoral]] [[fellow]]ship at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] in the laboratory of Ann Hirsch between 2012 and 2014. While at UCLA, she was also a fellow in the Department of Design and Media Arts at the Art|Sci Center.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2013/05/the-biotic-woman/309280/|title=The Hordes of Microbes Inside Your Body Are Your Friends|last=Madrigal|first=Alexis C.|date=2013-04-24|website=The Atlantic|language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-21}}</ref>

=== Bioengineering and bioart ===
Agapakis is now the Creative Director of the Boston-based biotechnology company [[Ginkgo Bioworks]], known as "The Organism Company," which specializes in genetically engineering organisms like yeast and bacteria for a number of applications—from engineering perfumes and food to engineering solutions for more sustainable agriculture.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/stephaniemlee/ginkgo-bioworks-fundraising|title=Ginkgo Bioworks, The Latest "Unicorn," Genetically Engineers Everything From Perfume To Food|website=BuzzFeed News|date=14 December 2017 |language=en|access-date=2018-12-21}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> One project, for example, focuses on engineering yeast to produce a rose-like scent by modifying their genes to produce the molecules a rose makes to generate that scent.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thisismold.com/process/manufacture/ginkgo-bioworks-christina-agapakis|title=Organism Designers at Ginkgo Bioworks are Designing Tasty Food Flavors|website=MOLD :: Designing the Future of Food|date=21 September 2017|language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-21}}</ref> The rose oil fragrance was licensed to the fragrance maker [[Robertet]].<ref name="cosmeticsdesign.com">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cosmeticsdesign.com/Article/2015/11/03/Ginkgo-Bioworks-and-Robertet-to-develop-new-fragrance-ingredients|title=Ginkgo Bioworks and Robertet to develop new fragrance ingredients|last=cosmeticsdesign.com|website=cosmeticsdesign.com|date=3 November 2015 |language=en-GB|access-date=2018-12-22}}</ref> Agapakis has also been leading the company's 100 Vial Project, which is engineering a library of bio-based scents. One of these scents is an effort to resurrect the smell of a long-extinct flower by analyzing preserved botanical samples to identify the DNA encoding smell-producing enzymes. They can then engineer yeast to produce those same enzymes and produce the molecules that create the extinct flower's scent.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Agapakis|first1=Christina|last2=Lee|first2=Suzanne|date=2018-09-19|title=Design With Science|url=https://jods.mitpress.mit.edu/pub/issue4-agapakis-lee|journal=Journal of Design and Science|language=en}}</ref> The project is in collaboration with Agapakis's long-time collaborator [[Sissel Tolaas]] and Daisy Ginsberg.

In her role as Creative Director, Agapakis focuses on creating experiences and communicating stories about the bioengineering work the company undertakes with the ultimate goal of making biotechnology more approachable.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/katherynthayer/2016/12/21/this-scientist-explains-complex-biotech-with-food-art-and-empathy/|title=This Scientist Explains Complex Biotech With Food, Art And Empathy|last=Thayer|first=Katheryn|website=Forbes|language=en|access-date=2018-12-21}}</ref> For instance, Ginkgo hosted designer Natsai Audrey Chieza as artist in residence to experiment with dying textiles with bacteria as an environmentally sound and resource-conservative approach alternative to commercial dyes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mentalfloss.com/article/504090/artist-screen-prints-fabrics-bacteria|title=Artist Screen-Prints Fabrics With Bacteria|date=2017-08-31|website=mentalfloss.com|language=en|access-date=2018-12-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2018/02/ginkgo-bioworks-gmos/552374/|title=Can This Company Convince You to Love GMOs?|last=Zhang|first=Sarah|date=2018-02-12|website=The Atlantic|language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-22}}</ref>

=== Science writing ===
Agapakis is also a science writer. She began blogging in graduate school and in 2011 started a column for [[Scientific American]] called the "Oscillator," sharing her thoughts on the latest developments in the field of synthetic biology for a popular audience.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/network-central/introducing-sciamblogs-bloggers-christina-agapakis/|title=Introducing #SciAmBlogs bloggers: Christina Agapakis|last=Zivkovic|first=Bora|website=Scientific American Blog Network|language=en|access-date=2018-12-22}}</ref> Her posts covered a number of topics from [[sustainability]] to the intersection between art and science to the microbiology of body fluids.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/oscillator/|title=Oscillator|website=Scientific American Blog Network|language=en|access-date=2018-12-22}}</ref> She has also written for a variety of outlets, including highlighting the women who made microbiology possible for [[Popular Science]] and reviewing Sophia Roosth's book ''Synthetic: How life got made'' for [[New Scientist]].<ref name="cosmeticsdesign.com"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg23431260-600-synthetic-biologys-ties-to-our-humanity-let-it-elude-definition/|title=Synthetic biology's ties to our humanity let it elude definition|last=Agapakis|first=Christina|website=New Scientist|language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-22}}</ref> She also co-founded a four-edition print science magazine called ''Method Quarterly'' about how science works in practice with science writers Azeen Ghorayshi and [[Rose Eveleth]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.methodquarterly.com/|title=Method {{!}} Science in the making|language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-22}}</ref>
